questions.question: One positive allocation amount appears 10 times under the same PAP across three offices. Which review alarm rings?
questions.explanation: This exact amount/PAP pattern meets the repeated-allocation screen’s occurrence and named-office thresholds. It is a pattern to inspect, not proof of duplicate work.

questions.hint: Same amount, same PAP, several offices.

questions.question: A project title appears again in an older GAA, with the same location and no detected scope conflict. Which flag describes the pattern?
questions.explanation: The historical screen compares normalized full titles and qualified locations, while excluding detected direction, location, tranche, or disjoint-chainage conflicts. A recurrence is a review lead, not proof of duplicate work.

sources.label: HGAB 3rd · review queue flag definitions and counts

questions.hint: It describes a project title recurring in a prior GAA.

questions.question: A road project’s station range overlaps an older funded range. Which flag fits?
questions.explanation: The overlap screen records intersecting stated chainage for a human to compare the original funded scopes. Overlap can have a legitimate explanation.

sources.label: HGAB 3rd · review queue flag definitions and counts

questions.hint: Look for the flag named after station-range evidence.

questions.question: For a project to trigger the HGAB high-rate flag, what must its rate exceed?
choices: Any rate in the top half
questions.explanation: The project rate must exceed both twice the peer median and Q3 + 1.5 × IQR. This is a review signal, not proof of overpricing.

sources.label: HGAB 3rd · review queue flag definitions and counts

questions.hint: The screen uses two tests together.

questions.question: What stated road length triggers the separate very-short-range review flag?
questions.explanation: A recovered printed length below 10 meters triggers a denominator-warning flag so the range notation and funded extent can be checked.

sources.label: HGAB 3rd · review queue flag definitions and counts

questions.hint: It is a short denominator warning, not a price finding.

questions.question: When can a rehabilitation project receive the prior-condition review flag?
questions.explanation: The screen requires a full-range match and a dated pre-budget Good/Fair assessment. Later deterioration or different scope may still justify work.

sources.label: HGAB 3rd · review queue flag definitions and counts

questions.hint: The condition evidence needs a date and full-range coverage.

questions.question: A House-version project row has no selected one-to-one NEP match. What does the flag invite reviewers to check?
questions.explanation: The matcher did not select an NEP counterpart. Title or scope variation can explain that, so the row stays a review candidate.

sources.label: HGAB 3rd · review queue flag definitions and counts

questions.hint: It is a matching-screen result, not a final finding.

questions.question: The DPWH Transparency snapshot has no matched document listing for a project. What can you safely conclude?
questions.explanation: The flag describes what is absent from the captured snapshot. It does not prove that documents do not exist elsewhere.

sources.label: HGAB 3rd · review queue flag definitions and counts

questions.hint: Keep the conclusion as narrow as the snapshot.

questions.question: In the HGAB 3rd-reading bridge table, which project has the highest allocation per stated meter?
questions.explanation: The Burol Overpass entry has a ₱150 million allocation and a 25 m stated chainage, or ₱6 million per stated meter—the highest among the bridge entries with usable stated lengths in this dataset. The chainage may include approaches, and allocation per meter is a screening ratio, not construction unit cost.
questions.hint: Compare each allocation with its stated meters. Burol’s title gives Sta. 1+120 to Sta. 1+145.

questions.question: Burol’s bridge-rate card shows ₱150 million across 25 stated meters. What allocation per stated meter does that work out to?
questions.explanation: ₱150 million divided by 25 stated meters is ₱6 million per stated meter. The chainage may include approaches, so this is a screening ratio, not construction unit cost.
questions.hint: Divide the allocation by 25.

questions.question: A project beats its peer median by 2×, but stays below Q3 + 1.5× IQR. Does it trigger the high-rate flag?
choices: Only if it is a bridge
questions.explanation: The screen requires the rate to exceed both thresholds. Even when it triggers, it is a review lead, not proof of overpricing.
questions.hint: The rule uses two checks together.

questions.question: A road title gives an 8-meter segment. Which review signal should light up?
questions.explanation: The separate short-range screen flags stated lengths under 10 meters for source review. It asks a human to check the notation and scope.
questions.hint: Eight is below the disclosed 10-meter review threshold.

questions.question: The same positive amount appears 10 times under one PAP across three offices. Which review flag catches this pattern?
questions.explanation: The repeated-amount screen looks for the same positive amount under one PAP across at least three named offices. It highlights a pattern for review; it does not explain why the amounts match.
questions.hint: Look for the flag about an amount appearing again and again.

questions.question: A project has a POW and geotagged photos, but no RDC endorsement. What does the documentation screen call this?
questions.explanation: The documentation screen treats a missing POW, photos, or RDC endorsement as incomplete documentation for review.
questions.hint: One of the tracked document types is still missing.

questions.question: An HGAB 3rd-reading project has no selected counterpart in the matching screen and no listed documents. Which two review leads apply?
choices: No selected counterpart and missing documentation
questions.answer: No selected counterpart and missing documentation
questions.explanation: The row merits both a counterpart review and a document-listing check. Neither condition alone establishes a new project or missing work.
questions.hint: One signal is about the comparison set; the other is about the document record.

sources.label: HGAB 3rd · matching and documentation review queue

questions.question: A road is budgeted for rehabilitation, and its full matched range was rated Good/Fair in a known pre-budget year. Which review lead fits?
questions.explanation: The condition screen gives a point only for rehabilitation/reconstruction/major repair on a fully matched range assessed Good/Fair in a known pre-budget year. Later deterioration or different funded components may justify the work.
questions.hint: The clue is a dated condition rating covering the whole matched range.

sources.label: HGAB 3rd · review flag evidence and definitions

questions.question: A pavement-work project has a full matched range with a recorded surfacing year within five budget years. Which review lead appears?
questions.explanation: The screen flags pavement work when the full matched range has a positive recorded last-surfacing year within five budget years. Old inventories may miss later works, so this remains a review lead.
questions.hint: The clue is a recent recorded pavement surface on the same full range.

sources.label: HGAB 3rd · review flag evidence and definitions

questions.question: The local attachment check finds photos and an RDC endorsement, but no POW. Which documentation flag applies?
questions.explanation: Each missing document type among locally inspected attachment lists can receive its own documentation flag. An uninspected record stays unknown.
questions.hint: Two document types are present; identify the absent third type.

sources.label: HGAB 3rd · review flag evidence and definitions

questions.question: The local attachment check finds a POW and RDC endorsement, but no geotagged photos. Which documentation flag applies?
questions.explanation: Missing geotagged photos can receive a separate documentation flag when the attachment list was locally inspected. An uninspected record stays unknown.
questions.hint: The POW and RDC are present; look for the absent visual evidence.

sources.label: HGAB 3rd · review flag evidence and definitions

questions.question: How many district-office Rainwater Collector System lines remained unchanged in the HGAB 3rd-reading trace?
questions.explanation: The stage trace found 199 district-office RCS lines unchanged in HGAB 3rd reading. Each retained a ₱4.2 million allocation; the comparison describes budget stages, not expenditure.
questions.hint: Compare what each proposal lists with the repeated allocation.

questions.question: An HGAB 3rd-reading multi-purpose building has no selected NEP counterpart. What should a reviewer compare before calling it new?
choices: Whether its title uses capital letters
questions.explanation: The counterpart review considers title, office, location, and scope; an unmatched row alone does not establish a new project.
questions.hint: A reliable match needs more than one text string.

questions.question: An HGAB 3rd-reading project title recurs in an older GAA. What should be compared before calling the work a duplicate?
questions.explanation: Compare location, scope, quantities, and chainage against the historical entry. A repeated title is a lead for review, not proof of duplicate work.
questions.hint: Check whether it is the same place and the same funded segment.

questions.question: A large named appropriation returns in the budget. Which record would best explain its full history?
choices: A whole-project cost and completion ledger
questions.answer: A whole-project cost and completion ledger
questions.explanation: A whole-project ledger can show prior appropriations, cumulative costs, completed components, and what remains to be funded.
questions.hint: Follow the project from its first appropriation through completion.

questions.question: A project has no supported segment length. What should the cost-per-meter screen do?
questions.explanation: Without a supported length, an allocation-per-meter rate cannot be calculated. The missing denominator is an evidence gap, not a zero-length project.
questions.hint: A rate needs a defensible denominator.

questions.question: A bridge ranks high per stated meter. What should a reviewer check before interpreting that ratio?
choices: Funded span, approaches, and project quantities
Whether the ratio is the largest
questions.answer: Funded span, approaches, and project quantities
questions.explanation: Stated chainage may include approaches, and the full allocation may cover more than the bridge span. Width, structure, quantities, and funded extent are needed for interpretation.
questions.hint: Check what the allocation covers and what the stated denominator measures.

sources.label: Cost per meter · bridge scope and method

questions.question: The Camayse–Mualbual road in Zumarraga is 1,016 m long and appears in the high-rate review queue. Its listed allocation rate is about how many times the peer median?
questions.explanation: The queue lists ₱118,110.24 per stated meter against a ₱22,727.27 peer median, or 5.2×. The screen is a review lead; the funded scope and quantities still need checking.
questions.hint: Compare ₱118,110.24 with the peer median of ₱22,727.27.

questions.question: Barangay Tutuloy’s 2027 road title covers Sta. 0+000–0+798. The matched 2026 title covers Sta. 0+000–0+524.40. How much stated range overlaps?

questions.question: A rehabilitation entry for Manila North Road in Pampanga matches a recorded Fair/Good condition assessment. What year is that assessment dated?
questions.explanation: The queue records a full-range Fair/Good assessment from 2025. Conditions can change, and the assessment does not establish that the proposed work is unnecessary.
